entry.title: How to Organize a Corporate Event: The Complete 12-Week Checklist (with 2026 Costs)
entry.content:
In short: running a well-executed corporate event is a matter of timeline, not budget — 12 weeks spread across 6 phases cover everything you need. This checklist, with typical 2026 costs, works for kick-offs, conventions, town halls and team building events from 30 to 500 attendees. Follow it in order, delegate each item to the right owner, and on event day you’ll manage surprises — not chase the obvious.

The 12 weeks in 6 phases

The 12-week structure isn’t arbitrary: it reflects the real time it takes between the strategic decision, signing supplier contracts, internal communication, and operations on event day. Compressing it below 8 weeks introduces genuine risk on venue and catering.

Phase 1 — Strategic setup (weeks 12-10): objective, budget, in-house-vs-agency decision. No suppliers until you’ve answered these three questions.

Phase 2 — Key suppliers (weeks 9-8): venue signed, caterer briefed, AV booked. The best suppliers sell out 8 weeks ahead on popular dates (Thursday-Friday, end of quarter).

Phase 3 — Communication and registration (weeks 7-6): save-the-date, registration page live, form finalized. From this point attendees exist as structured data.

Phase 4 — Detailed logistics (weeks 5-4): final numbers to the caterer, printed materials in production, speakers briefed on slides and timing.

Phase 5 — Pre-go-live (weeks 3-2): reminder email sequence, staff coordination, on-site AV tech test, timed agenda dry-run.

Phase 6 — Go-live (week 1 + event day + post): daily checklist, arrivals management, on-the-fly directing, post-event survey within 24 hours.

Weeks 12-10 — Strategic setup

Event objective

Before choosing a venue, you need a clear answer to: why are we running this event? The four corporate macro-objectives have very different formats:

  • Kick-off (motivate, align on annual priorities): plenary with a stage, internal speakers, an interactive session. Duration: half a day + lunch.
  • Town hall (inform on results, organizational changes): theatre-style room, streaming for remote offices, structured Q&A. Duration: 2-3 hours.
  • Convention (align the sales team, launch a product): plenary + breakout sessions, networking, often a closing dinner.
  • Team building (cohesion, onboarding): an unusual venue, a facilitator, structured activities. Duration: half a day or more.

Write the objective in a single line with at least one number. If you can’t, the event isn’t ready yet.

Budget allocation

A standard formula for corporate events in 2026:

  • 40% venue + catering
  • 25% AV (audio, video, lighting, directing)
  • 15% communication + printed materials + swag
  • 10% staff + registration platform
  • 10% contingency — untouchable until event day

In-house vs agency decision

In-house pays off with a dedicated owner, recurring events, and suppliers already under contract — estimated savings of 15-30%. An agency pays off for strategic one-off events, a complex venue, VIP speakers, or when nobody has ever organized an event over 100 people (a 12-20% premium on budget, but it offloads the operational risk).

Weeks 9-8 — Venue and key suppliers

Venue selection criteria

Four non-negotiable filters, in order of elimination:

  1. Certified capacity — the figure on the occupancy certificate, not the one that’s advertised. Ask for the document.
  2. Accessibility — parking (spaces vs expected cars), public transport within 10 minutes, certified disabled access.
  3. Included technology — built-in audio, stable data network, projector or LED wall. Anything missing has to be rented and adds a risk variable.
  4. Time constraints — the load-in window (can you get in at 7:00?) and load-out (are you out by 22:00?).

Sign with a deposit and a written cancellation clause — verbal cancellations don’t exist in legal terms.

Catering: choosing and briefing

Three formats and average costs:

  • Standing buffet: networking, flexible use of space — €25-45/person
  • Seated lunch: high perceived quality, mandatory for conventions — €40-70/person
  • Evening cocktail: informal close — €30-55/person

At the briefing: hand over the attendee count +10%, service times, and space constraints. Dietary restrictions: a detailed list 5 days in advance, not on the day itself.

AV: what to ask for, what to avoid

Three rules you can’t compress:

  • Always have a backup — a second microphone, a spare projector for critical keynotes, a spare HDMI cable.
  • On-site sound check — in the actual room, with the actual chairs, on event day or the evening before. Never “we already tested it yesterday”.
  • A full-time AV technician if you have video, multiple speakers or programmed transitions — €200-500/day, and it’s not a luxury.

Weeks 7-6 — Communication and registration

Save-the-date

Send it 8-10 weeks ahead, as soon as the venue is locked. It contains only three elements: date, title, CTA (register / add to calendar). No agenda, no speakers, no details that aren’t confirmed yet — every change after sending is internal reputational damage.

Registration platform (no excuses, even for internal events)

Above 50 attendees, a Google Form means manual confirmations, check-in with a printed sheet, and no structured data on no-shows. A dedicated platform solves all of that in an hour of setup. To understand what separates a serious tool from a mediocre one, read the online ticketing guide — the criteria apply to free internal events too.

Four minimum features for corporate events:

  • Automatic email confirmation with a QR code
  • Real-time attendee dashboard
  • Smartphone check-in
  • CSV export with filters for dietary, department and status

The form: what to collect (and what NOT to collect)

Collect: first and last name, work email, department, dietary restrictions (dropdown, not free text), swag size if applicable.

Don’t collect: mobile number (unless you’re sending SMS), physical address, any data you won’t use operationally.

Every extra field lowers the completion rate by 3-7%: for 200 attendees, 8 useless fields generate 15-30 drop-offs you’ll have to recover manually.

Weeks 5-4 — Detailed logistics

Catering: final numbers

Five weeks out, your registration data is stable. Give the caterer the final number + a 5% buffer (never less, never more than 10% — beyond 10% it becomes unrecoverable cost). The rule is simple: better 8 extra portions than 3 people without a meal.

Dietary restrictions, operationally

Three steps, in this order:

  1. CSV export from the registration platform — filter by the dietary field and send it to the catering contact 5 days in advance.
  2. A badge with a symbol for attendees with documented restrictions — a triangle, a leaf, a color code: floor staff recognize it without reading the name.
  3. Floor staff briefing the morning of the event — 15 minutes, show the badge, explain the procedure. Don’t delegate it to the caterer and hope they handle it on their own.

Printed materials and speaker briefing

Production lead times: badges 4-5 working days (first name, last name, department, role color code), program and signage 3-4 days, custom swag 3-4 weeks — order the last of these first.

Speaker briefing: send the slide template (1920×1080, 16:9), the exact duration (“20 minutes, Q&A excluded”), the file delivery method, and the AV tech contact for embedded video/audio at least 3 weeks ahead.

Weeks 3-2 — Pre-go-live

Reminders and email sequence

The optimal sequence in three steps, each with incremental information:

  • 7 days before: full logistics briefing — exact address, parking map, recommended check-in time, dress code if required, what to bring.
  • 24 hours before: final email — personal QR link, on-site contact phone number, reminder of the plenary start time.

Don’t send generic reminders with no new information: they lower the open rate of the ones that follow.

Staff coordination

Create a shift table with: name, role (welcome, check-in desk, room, directing), arrival time, phone contact. Print it and hand it out physically. Don’t rely on WhatsApp alone.

Minimum staff for a 100-person event:

  • 2 people at the check-in desk (one scans, one handles exceptions)
  • 1 room lead (coordinates audio and speakers)
  • 1 general coordinator (you or the project lead — don’t try to do both)

AV technical test

The on-site test should use the same configuration as event day: same screen, same speaker laptop, same microphone. Test specifically:

  • [ ] Audio handoff from laptop to room system
  • [ ] Embedded video in slides (often the source of problems)
  • [ ] Lavalier microphone + backup
  • [ ] Internet connection for any live demos
  • [ ] Remote slide control (who has it? does it work?)

Agenda dry-run

Simulate the entire day with a stopwatch. Every session, every break, every transition. The real agenda always has 15-20% of hidden slack that only surfaces in this phase — better to find it now than live. See also the article on mistakes to avoid in event planning for the most common agenda patterns.

Week 1 — Operational go-live

A daily checklist for the last 7 days before the event:

  • [ ] Day -7: written confirmation to all suppliers (venue, catering, AV, external staff)
  • [ ] Day -7: reminder email to attendees (see sequence above)
  • [ ] Day -6: verify the final headcount from the registration dashboard
  • [ ] Day -5: send the final dietary list to the caterer
  • [ ] Day -5: send badges to print production
  • [ ] Day -4: receive printed materials and check quality
  • [ ] Day -3: on-site AV technical test (if not already done in week -2)
  • [ ] Day -2: staff briefing with assigned shifts and roles
  • [ ] Day -2: upload the final attendee list to the check-in platform
  • [ ] Day -1: final reminder to attendees (24 hours before)
  • [ ] Day -1: recharge all check-in devices, print a paper backup list
  • [ ] Event morning: set up the desk within 60 minutes of doors opening, brief staff 30 minutes before arrivals

Event day

Morning — Setup and briefing

Arrive on-site 90 minutes before doors open. In this order: (1) sign the handover with the venue manager, (2) place signage from the entrance to the desk, (3) brief staff for 15 minutes on roles and the alert code, (4) test check-in with 2-3 sample QR codes, (5) confirm timing and the final number with the caterer.

Arrivals and check-in

Check-in is the first physical impression — and often the one that sticks. Target: under 90 seconds per person with a digital QR and 2 operators. If the event has breakout sessions or staggered entries, set up time-slot management in advance to avoid bottlenecks in the first half hour.

Plan B: a paper list by surname letter, printed in the morning — it doesn’t replace the digital flow, but it saves the day if the connection drops.

During the event — Directing and surprises

The coordinator shouldn’t be in the room: they should be within sight of the directing position and the desk. Typical surprises, in order of frequency:

  • A late speaker (a 5-minute buffer between sessions)
  • Audio dropping out (the AV tech reachable, not “out at lunch”)
  • An attendee without a badge (check-in recovers them by name)
  • Late catering (the room lead’s direct number)

Wrap-up

Tear down the check-in desks 30 minutes before the planned end. Export the attendance CSV from the dashboard before powering off the devices — it’s the data for your report and survey.

Post-event — 72 hours

The 72 hours afterwards matter as much as the 12 weeks of preparation. Three mandatory actions:

Within 24 hours — NPS survey by email. A form of 3 questions max: NPS (0-10 scale), one open question on what worked, one on what to improve. For every extra hour you wait, the response rate drops 5-8%. Target: response rate >35%, NPS >30 points.

Within 48 hours — Follow-up with materials. Email attendees with: slides (if the speaker has consented), selected photos, and any links or resources mentioned during the sessions. This step turns an event into a reference point — people come back to the email when they’re looking for that resource.

Within 72 hours — Internal retrospective brief. A 30-minute meeting with the organizing team. Three questions: what worked (to repeat), what didn’t (to drop), and what to do differently. Write the points down somewhere — otherwise the next event starts from scratch.

Keep all the documentation (contracts, attendee exports, final budget) in a shared folder labeled by date — whoever organizes the next event at the company will thank you.

Typical 2026 costs — summary table

A reference for a single-day convention, 100 attendees, venue not included in the package.

Item Range € Notes
Venue 1,500 – 4,000 Standard conference rooms; historic villas and exhibition centres double this
Catering (buffet/lunch) 4,000 – 8,000 €40-80/person; evening cocktail -30%
AV (audio, video, lighting) 1,500 – 4,000 Includes on-site tech; LED wall adds €1,500-3,000
Registration / ticketing 0 – 500 Monthly SaaS or per-event fee; sometimes bundled in an HR subscription
Communication and badges 300 – 1,000 Badge, program and signage printing; swag excluded
Swag / materials 500 – 3,000 Highly variable; optional
External staff 500 – 1,500 2-3 hosts or check-in operators for one day
Contingency (10%) 1,000 – 2,200 Untouchable until event day
Typical total 10,000 – 18,000 All-inclusive, premium swag excluded

Under 50 attendees or for half days, the total drops to €5,000-9,000. Above 200 attendees, the scale isn’t linear: AV and logistics grow faster than the per-head cost.

Mistakes that cost dearly in B2B

Five corporate-specific anti-patterns, in order of impact:

1. Underestimating check-in. With a paper list: 3-5 minutes/person. For 100 people in 30 minutes you’d need 10-17 operators — or you start late in front of everyone. With a QR and 2 operators: 90 seconds, 100 people in 25 minutes. It’s not a detail — it’s the perception attendees carry for the entire day.

2. No plan B for AV. The projector that won’t turn on, the HDMI that won’t talk, the microphone that squeals: none of these are rare. A €15,000 event gets remembered for a broken microphone in the first 10 minutes. The backup doesn’t cost anything — what costs is not having it.

3. Catering without a structured dietary list. “10% have restrictions” isn’t enough if you don’t know which ones. A predefined dropdown in the registration form (vegan, gluten-free, lactose-free, other) costs nothing and prevents the awkward situation of a coeliac attendee facing a standard buffet.

4. An agenda that’s too dense. “15-minute coffee break” in a compressed agenda becomes 8 real minutes — people don’t get up, they reach for their phones. A 20% buffer makes the agenda look more professional than one that runs and slips. The timed dry-run is the only way to catch it in advance.

5. Zero post-event survey. Without data, the next event starts from informal opinions. A 3-question NPS sent within 24 hours gives you a measurable baseline for every subsequent edition — 10 minutes of setup, with a higher ROI than the entire organization effort.

Conclusion

The difference between a corporate event that leaves a positive mark and one that ends up as “a wasted day” isn’t the budget — it’s how you structure the 12 weeks beforehand. Each phase adds incremental value: the strategic phase defines the scope, logistics reduce risk, and communication brings the right people into the right room with the right expectations.

A registration platform that handles automatic confirmations, dietary restrictions, smartphone check-in and a live dashboard takes 80% of the micro-headaches off your plate — the ones that otherwise land on your shoulders on event day, when you have other things to do.

entry.title: How to Promote an Event: 9 Channels That Actually Work (with 2026 Numbers)
entry.content:
In short: nine channels genuinely work for promoting an event, but not all at once and not for every event type. The classic winning sequence is: your own list + partners, then organic social, then paid ads and local PR. The key is to measure every channel with UTMs and calculate the CAC (cost of acquisition) per source. Without measurement, event marketing is blind: you know how many tickets you sold, but not why — and you can’t replicate the result.

The timing of your promotion

Before you switch on any channel, you need to understand when and in what order to use it. The rule of thumb that works best in practice is the 60-40-20:

  • 60% of your audience should be reached in the early phase, more than four weeks before the event. These are your early adopters, the most motivated: low acquisition cost, no need to manufacture urgency.
  • 40% mid-funnel, between two and four weeks out: a broader audience that needs more nudges (retargeting, reminders, social proof from people who have already signed up).
  • 20% last-call, the final 48 hours: lean on urgency and scarcity. This phase pays for itself with a conversion spike, but it doesn’t replace the first two — it arrives too late for anyone who has already decided to ignore the event.

Timing also depends on ticket price. For the technical setup that lets you take registrations the moment you launch — page live, payments active, automatic confirmation — see the online ticketing guide: it’s best to have everything ready at least three weeks before the public launch.

Event type Recommended lead time
Free event 3-6 weeks
Paid event < €50 6-10 weeks
Paid event > €100 or B2B 12-16 weeks

Channel 1 — Your own email list

This is the channel with the lowest cost per acquisition of all nine. If you already have a list of contacts interested in your topic, every email you send costs essentially nothing and converts better than any ad.

Industry average numbers for events:

Metric Benchmark
Open rate 25-40%
CTR on the registration link 2-5%
Final conversion (click → ticket) 2-8%

A typical sequence for a paid event involves at least three emails:

  1. Save the date (registration opens): a clean announcement, early-bird pricing, a direct link to the page.
  2. Reminder + value (-10 days): one more reason to come — a speaker, the agenda, a testimonial from a past attendee.
  3. Last call (-48 hours): real urgency (remaining seats, early-bird about to expire, or a price increase).

For segmentation, separate your engaged contacts (opened at least 2 emails in the last 90 days) from the cold ones. Email the engaged first, with direct subject lines. For the cold segment, use curiosity-gap subject lines and test on a small sample first.

Subject lines that work: “[Event name] — early-bird seats are running out” beats “Event X — register now” by roughly 30% in open rate, based on tests on a typical list.

Channel 2 — Partners & sponsors

A well-chosen partner can drive 20-40% of total registrations without spending a cent on ads. The mechanism is simple: you have something their audience values (content, a relationship, access), and they have a list that’s valuable to you.

How to pick the right partner:

  • An audience aligned with your target but not in direct competition with your core business
  • An active email list with an open rate above 20% (ask them up front — anyone who doesn’t know or won’t say is a red flag)
  • The ability to do active promotion, not just a link in a newsletter footer

The typical trade is a swap: you promote their content or event in your channels, and they do the same for you. If the value isn’t symmetrical (a much bigger partner), offer free access, a speaking slot, or co-branded visibility.

Tag every partner with separate UTMs (utm_source=partner-companyname&utm_medium=email). If a partner sends you 500 clicks from a qualified audience, that’s worth €500-1,500 of paid traffic — a measurable value you can bring to the table when negotiating the next event.

Channel 3 — Organic social

The most-used channel, but often the least efficient for anyone without an established community. The numbers are clear: organic reach of 5-15% of your followers, and a follower-to-registrant conversion of 0.3-1%.

With 2,000 Instagram followers you can expect 100-300 people exposed per post and 6-20 clicks to the registration page. It’s not your primary acquisition engine, but it keeps your existing audience warm and generates visible social proof.

By platform:

Platform Format that works Target audience
Instagram Reels (30-60s), Stories countdowns Consumer events, under 40
LinkedIn Text post + a question, native video B2B, professionals, HR
TikTok Native Reels, behind-the-scenes content Under 30, cultural events
Facebook Facebook Event, posts in industry groups Local community, over 35

Minimum frequency: one post every 3 days in the 3 weeks before the event. Don’t post only announcements — alternate value content (speaker previews, agenda teasers, audience questions) with direct registration posts.

Channel 4 — Meta Ads (Instagram + Facebook)

The first paid channel to test for consumer events. The advantage of Meta Ads is targeting by interests and behaviors: you can reach people who don’t follow you yet but who are statistically similar to your past attendees.

Average CPM: €5-15 depending on the sector and seasonal competition. With €30/day for 10 days you’ll have enough data to tell whether the channel works for your specific event.

Recommended targeting structure for events:

  1. Custom audience — upload your email list and past attendees. These are the people most likely to convert.
  2. Lookalike 2-5% from the custom audience — Meta finds similar profiles in the wider population.
  3. Interest stack — layer 3-5 interests related to your event (never just one, that’s too broad).

Formats that convert for events:

  • Reel/Video (6-15 seconds): high impressions, low CPM, great for awareness.
  • Carousel with 3-4 cards: speaker, agenda, venue — each card is one more reason to sign up.
  • Stories with a countdown sticker: visual urgency in the final 48 hours.

Always measure the cost per click to the registration page (CPC), not just impressions. A CPC above €2.50 for a consumer event under €50 is a sign of bad targeting or weak copy.

Channel 5 — Google Ads

Google Ads works for events only if there’s a relevant search query with meaningful volume. The question to ask before launching a campaign is: “what does someone who wants to attend an event like mine type into Google?”

When it makes sense to invest:

  • A B2B conference on a specific technical topic (“cybersecurity conference 2026”) — the query exists and intent is high.
  • A festival or consumer event with a recognizable brand (“[Festival name] tickets”) — people search for your name.
  • Competitive categories where you want to appear above your competitors.

When it’s a waste:

  • A generic consumer event (“things to do this Saturday”) — huge volume, very low intent, CPC burns budget without converting.
  • An ultra-niche event with an audience of a few hundred people in the whole country — the query doesn’t exist.

Suggested campaign structure: three separate groups — brand (your event’s name), non-brand (category + city), competitor (people already searching for similar events). Use phrase or exact match types, never broad on an event campaign with a limited budget.

Check search volume with Keyword Planner before investing: if your main query has fewer than 100 searches/month, Google Ads isn’t the right channel for you.

Channel 6 — LinkedIn Ads (B2B only)

LinkedIn Ads is the most expensive channel of all — average CPC €5-15, CPM between €30-80 — but it’s the only one that lets you target by job title, seniority, and industry with surgical precision.

It only makes sense to invest when your average ticket exceeds €300-500 and your typical attendee is a professional or decision-maker who needs to be convinced with rational arguments (ROI, credentials, headline speakers).

Targeting that works for B2B events:

  • Job title + seniority (e.g. “HR Manager”, “Operations Director”, “Senior” and above)
  • A specific industry (not “all industries” — that burns your budget)
  • Company size (e.g. 50-500 employees)

Formats: a Single Image Ad with longer copy and a concrete data point in the first line. The LinkedIn audience reads — it’s not the place for purely visual creativity. A message like “73% of CFOs can’t measure the ROI of training — we can. [Workshop, June 15]” converts better than a glossy banner.

Don’t test LinkedIn Ads with less than €500 of budget: below that threshold you won’t accumulate enough data to optimize.

Channel 7 — Local PR + traditional media

Often underrated, especially for consumer events with a strong local angle. An article in a local newspaper or regional edition is worth more than 10 Instagram posts in terms of perceived credibility and, indirectly, of SEO for your event.

How to increase your pickup rate:

  • Send the press release with 5-7 days of lead time before your desired publication date — local newsrooms have a short agenda but still work with a few days’ notice.
  • Include a local fact or data point that makes the story relevant to that specific outlet’s readers (“the first [category] event in [city] in three years”).
  • Offer a short interview (15 minutes by phone) to the journalist — a person is the narrative hook that local articles are always looking for.

Beyond print: industry blogs and niche podcasts are often willing to run a preview or an interview in exchange for a press pass or reserved seat. Identify the 3-5 with the audience best aligned to your event and reach out 3-4 weeks in advance.

The pickup rate (how many of your pitches turn into an article) is typically 20-40% for well-targeted local PR, and close to zero for generic releases blasted out indiscriminately.

Channel 8 — Early bird + early access

The early bird isn’t just a discount — it’s the main acquisition tool in the first weeks of promotion. People who buy early aren’t doing it to save money (the difference is often just €10-20): they do it because they’re already motivated, and the discount lowers the decision friction at a moment when the event still feels far off.

A typical structure that works:

  • A 20-30% discount off the full price, valid for the first 7 days of sales or the first 50 tickets (whichever comes first).
  • A visible timer on the registration page — not a fake countdown that resets, but a real timer with an expiry date and time.
  • An email reminder when 48 hours of early-bird remain, even if the person hasn’t bought yet.

In practice, the early bird alone unlocks 50-65% of registrations before the mid-funnel — it eases the pressure on the final week and gives you early signals on how well the event is performing.

To design a registration page with the early-bird timer positioned so it actually converts, see the guide on building an event registration page that converts: it has specific benchmarks on where to place the CTA and how to communicate scarcity without feeling contrived.

Channel 9 — Posters and flyers

For consumer events with a strong local geographic angle only. A summer festival in a mid-sized town, a market, a gig at a venue: physical posters reach people who aren’t searching for you online and will never see your Instagram post.

Where it works:

  • Bars and venues that match your demographic: €30-100 per location (printing + an arrangement with the venue), estimated conversion rate of 0.5-2% of foot traffic during the display period.
  • Flyers handed out at a similar prior event: if you attend, as a sponsor or simple visitor, an event with a comparable audience, 500 flyers generate a 3-8% QR scan rate — the contact is already warm.
  • Partner materials (lounges, waiting areas, sports club locker rooms): heavily dependent on audience alignment.

Operational rule for measurement: use QR codes with a different UTM for each location (utm_source=flyer&utm_medium=print&utm_campaign=event-xyz&utm_content=bar-name). Without separate UTMs, you’ll know the flyers “maybe” worked, but you’ll have no proof.

A realistic budget for a local poster campaign (20-30 locations): €200-600 all in. It’s not the channel for big numbers, but it’s excellent for generating qualified local awareness at predictable fixed costs.

Measurement: UTMs, GA4, CAC per channel

All nine channels above become data only with measurement. And without data, every decision about your next event is a guess — often an expensive one.

The minimum UTM structure for every link:

utm_source     → channel (email, instagram, linkedin, partner-companyname, google)
utm_medium     → type (email, social, paid, referral, print)
utm_campaign   → event name (e.g. workshop-hr-june-2026)
utm_content    → variant (e.g. earlybird, reminder, last-call, reel-v1)

Every link that leaves your channels should carry UTMs — including links in social bios, organic posts, and partner emails. A link without UTMs is a ticket sold whose origin you’ll never know.

In GA4, set up a specific conversion event for “ticket purchase completed” (or “registration completed” for free events). GA4 attributes the conversion to the last session with UTMs — not perfect, but good enough for budget decisions.

CAC per channel formula:

Channel CAC = total channel spend / tickets attributed to that channel (via UTM)

A concrete example: if you spent €400 on Meta Ads and got 32 registrations with utm_source=instagram, your Instagram CAC is €12.50. Compare it to the average ticket value (€40): ROAS = 3.2×. Below 4× means that channel is operating at a loss relative to the event’s margin.

Not measuring isn’t a neutral choice — it’s one of the most expensive mistakes in event management, as we describe in our list of mistakes to avoid in event organization.

A sample sequence for a 300-attendee event

Here’s the week-by-week operational sequence for a paid consumer event (€40 ticket) targeting 300 registrations. Starting 12 weeks before the event.

Week Priority action
-12 Page live, early bird active. Save-the-date email to your own list. Partner agreements activated.
-10 Organic social posts 3×/week. First email to partners for a promotion swap.
-8 Launch Meta Ads retargeting page visitors + lookalike of the email list. Budget €30/day.
-6 Check early-bird conversion (target: 40% of tickets sold). If below, accelerate list emails.
-5 Early-bird reminder email “last 7 days”. Local PR activated (press release).
-4 Early bird closes. Switch to full price. “Sold XX tickets” post for social proof.
-3 Raise Meta Ads budget to €50/day. Podcast/industry-blog outreach.
-2 Mid-funnel email with speaker/agenda content. Instagram Reels teasers.
-1 Last-call email + 48-hour timer. Stories countdown. Possible Google Ads brand campaign on the event name.
Day 0 Check remaining capacity. “Few seats left” only if true — fake scarcity burns the list.

The critical checkpoints are at week -6 (are you at 40%?) and week -2 (are you at 80%?). If you’re behind, the fastest lever is almost always your own email list with a fresh incentive, not bumping the ads budget, which needs 3-5 days to optimize.

Conclusion

Promoting an event doesn’t mean running all nine channels at once — it means figuring out which three or four work for your event type, your budget, and your timing, and executing them well.

The sequence that works for most events: start with your own list and partners (zero or near-zero cost), add the early bird to open sales fast, then scale with paid ads only once you already have real conversion data from the page.

Every channel has a different cost, conversion rate, and ramp-up curve — the one unrecoverable mistake is not measuring. entry.title: How to Build an Event Registration Page That Converts
entry.content:
In short: an event registration page converts when it answers three questions within 5 seconds — what the event is, who it’s for, why now — and when it removes technical friction from the sign-up path. This guide covers structure, form, copy, social proof and hard benchmarks. By the end you’ll know what to test first on your current page.

The registration page is a funnel, not a showcase

30-60% of visitors to an event registration page leave without completing it. Not because they aren’t interested — they got there precisely because the event appeals to them — but because the page doesn’t remove enough friction between interest and action.

The right metaphor isn’t “a showcase that displays the event” but “a funnel that turns a visitor into an attendee”. And like every funnel, each step has a measurable, improvable conversion rate. The metrics that govern everything are:

  1. External CTR: % of visitors who reach the page vs. clicks on the campaign/link
  2. Scroll depth: % who get at least as far as the form (typically halfway down the page)
  3. Form completion rate: % who fill in and submit the form
  4. Post-checkout rate: % who also complete payment (for paid events)

Improve each of these four metrics by 10% and you get 46% more registrations from the same traffic. That’s why optimizing the page is almost always more profitable than spending more on ads.

What the page must do in the first 5 seconds

The first test for any page is: if a visitor lands and scrolls for 5 seconds, do they understand what they’re looking at? If the answer is no, half the traffic is already lost.

The 4 pieces of information that must be absorbable in 5 seconds:

  1. What the event is (type: conference, workshop, open day, concert)
  2. When (exact date, in a clear format — “15 November 2026”, not “15.11.26”)
  3. Where (city + venue, or “Online” made obvious)
  4. Who it’s for (a clear target — “for HR leaders at companies of 50-500 employees” beats “for professionals”)

To these you often add:

  1. How much it costs (or “free”, visibly)
  2. Primary call to action (the button you see right away, not on screen two)

If you’re designing a new page, print your hero section and show it to someone for 5 seconds. Ask them to repeat in their own words: what, when, where, who for. If they can’t, rewrite the hero before you touch the form.

Anatomy of a registration page that converts

There’s no single, universally optimal layout, but there is an architecture that works in more than 90% of cases. It’s made of 5 ordered blocks, each with a specific role.

Block 1 — Hero section (above the fold)

What it contains:

  • The event title in 1-2 lines max
  • A subtitle with one single sentence that communicates the value
  • Date + location, visible
  • A visible primary CTA (e.g. “Register for free”)
  • A context image or video (optional but useful)

What to avoid: generic claims like “the event of the year for innovators”, handshake stock photos, fake countdown timers.

Block 2 — Proof points (who’s there, what you’ll see)

Right below the hero, show concrete evidence:

  • Speakers with photo and affiliation
  • Sponsors (if relevant for credibility)
  • Logos from past editions or press mentions
  • Numbers (e.g. “340 decision-makers attended last year”)

Rule: never “we deliver a valuable experience” — always “here’s who was there last time and what they said”.

Block 3 — Agenda / content

3-6 bullet points describing what will happen, in operational language. Prefer concrete verbs (“you’ll learn how to…”, “you’ll meet…”, “you’ll see in a demo…”) over vague nouns (“quality networking”, “exclusive content”).

Block 4 — Registration form

The heart of the funnel. Details on its design in the dedicated section below.

Block 5 — FAQ + trust signals

6-10 frequently asked questions (refunds, dress code, parking, how to get in, certificate of attendance). Every answer prevents one more email to your support. Below the FAQ: privacy policy, contacts, and possibly the logos of payment and security systems.

A repeated second CTA at the bottom. Anyone who’s read this far is interested — don’t force them to scroll back up to find the button.

The form: fields, logic, progressive disclosure

The form is where most registrations are lost. Three guiding principles.

1. Fewer fields = more conversions (but above a minimum threshold)

Each extra field lowers the completion rate by 3-5%. But dropping below the operational minimum (e.g. name, email, GDPR consent) generates low-quality leads.

Recommended configuration by event type:

Event type Recommended fields
Free B2B webinar Name · Email · Company · Role · Consent (5)
Free in-person event Name · Email · City · Consent (4)
Paid B2C event Name · Email · City · Consent + payment details (5 + 3)
Paid B2B event with invoice Name · Email · Company · Tax/VAT ID · Address · Consent + payment (6 + 3)

Anything not strictly necessary at checkout should be deferred to a follow-up email one week before the event. This is mistake #5 we detailed in the guide to corporate event mistakes.

2. Progressive disclosure for complex forms

If your form has no choice but to carry 8+ fields (e.g. an educational event with billing details), split it into visible steps:

  • Step 1: Name, email, consent (“Continue”)
  • Step 2: Company, role, billing details (“Continue”)
  • Step 3: Payment (“Pay and confirm”)

A multi-step form with 8 fields spread across 3 steps converts 15-25% better than the same 8 fields in a single block. The psychological perception of “I’ve already done 2 out of 3” pushes people to finish.

3. Labels always visible, placeholders never used as labels

Never use the placeholder inside the field as the only label (e.g. <input placeholder="Email">). When the user clicks, the placeholder disappears, context is lost, errors go up. Labels belong above the field, always visible, never in faint grey.

Copy: 5 micro-optimizations that lift completion

Copy is underrated. Five small changes with measurable impact.

  1. CTA = verb + benefit: “Register for free” beats “Submit”. “Reserve your spot” beats “Sign up”.
  2. Highlight cost = zero when it’s free: “Free registration, no card required” reassures anyone afraid of finding traps in the form.
  3. Real countdown (only if it genuinely is): “60 of 100 spots left” works IF it’s true. If it’s fake scarcity, the brand gets called out on Reddit/forums within two weeks.
  4. Drop “Submit data”: it sounds bureaucratic and makes people think they’re sending sensitive information for no reason. Better: “Confirm registration”.
  5. Reassurance micro-copy under the CTA: a single line of 6-8 words (“You’ll get an email confirmation within 2 minutes”) raises conversion by 3-8% because it reduces uncertainty about “what happens next”.

Trust signals and social proof

A visitor to an event page is implicitly asking “can I trust this?”. Three pieces of evidence lower the trust threshold.

Testimonials from previous attendees

Not generic (“it was amazing!”) but specific:

“At last year’s edition I met 3 clients who are now in my pipeline. The return on the ticket price was immediate.” — Name, Role, Company

Real photos + an optional LinkedIn tag boost credibility.

Numbers from past editions

“340 attendees”, “4.7/5 NPS”, “12 countries represented”. Three specific numbers beat ten generic ones.

Logos with a concrete reference

Not “they chose us” but “they attend this series regularly”. A logo without context is decorative; a logo with a verifiable claim is credible.

Benchmarks: how much it really converts

How do you measure the result? Here are indicative benchmarks gathered from events with organic traffic + Meta/Google Ads campaigns:

Event type Conversion rate (visit → registration)
Free B2B webinar 35-55%
Free in-person B2B event 25-40%
Paid B2C event (ticket €20-50) 5-15%
Premium paid event (ticket >€200) 2-8%
Concert/cultural show 10-25%
Paid training course 8-20%

Below the benchmark means the page has structural problems. Above the benchmark means your traffic targeting is particularly qualified (nothing to optimize on the page — optimize for scale instead).

A/B tests: what to test first

If you already have a live page and want to optimize it, test in this order (expected average impact, decreasing):

  1. Hero headline → expected: ±15-30% on final completion
  2. CTA text and button color → expected: ±5-15%
  3. Number of form fields (reduce by 1-2) → expected: ±5-10%
  4. Price placement (visible right away vs. at the bottom) → expected: ±5-10%
  5. Social proof (add or change it) → expected: ±3-8%
  6. Video vs. hero image → expected: ±0-10% (depends on event type)

Keep the test running until statistical significance (minimum 300 conversions per variant). Don’t give in to the temptation to declare a winner after 50 registrations — the noise is too high.

Technical mistakes that silently kill conversion

Three invisible but devastating problems.

  1. Page not responsive on mobile — you lose 70% of traffic
  2. Load times over 3 seconds — you lose 30-40% before they even reach the form
  3. Form not working on Safari iOS — the classic scenario: a platform bug penalizes Apple users exclusively, and nobody notices for weeks

Always verify:

  • Test on a real iPhone (not just Chrome DevTools mobile emulation)
  • PageSpeed Insights above 85 on mobile
  • The final submit tested from a second browser with an empty cache

For a broader approach to structuring your ticketing platform as a whole, read our online ticketing guide. If your event has time slots or staggered entry, we have a dedicated operational guide.

Conclusion

An event registration page that converts isn’t a stroke of inspiration: it’s a series of 15-20 small design and copy decisions, each one testable and measurable. The good news is that you control all of them, and none of them costs direct money — they cost attention.

If you’re building a page from scratch, the platform does much of the structural work for you (mobile-optimized form, field validation, post-submit redirect, conversion tracking). Try Ticketto for free and create a test page to see whether the pattern works for you — feedback from a live page is worth more than ten articles read.

entry.title: Event Time Slots: How to Prevent Queues and Overcrowding
entry.content:
In short: time slots solve the number-one problem of capacity-limited events — endless queues — but they introduce management complexity you need to anticipate. This guide explains the three booking models, how to size your capacity, how to handle no-shows and overbooking, and what a platform must do to genuinely support the flow.

Why time slots are an underrated problem

Most organizers only think about time slots once the problem is already on the ground: “on open-day morning there was a 45-minute queue,” “we had to close the doors at noon because the exhibition was full.” By then the solution arrives long after the damage is done.

In reality, time slots are not an emergency tactic. They’re a way of shaping the experience from the start: you promise the attendee a certain level of comfort (no queues, no crowds, dedicated time) and you keep that promise by controlling density. Done well, it improves brand perception and pushes the event’s NPS up by 15–25%.

But badly designed slots are worse than no slots at all: someone who shows up at 10:00 only to discover they have to wait until 11:30 because “they booked that time but their slot fell through” will leave angry. This is where the difference lies between a system that works and one that’s just bureaucracy.

When you actually need them (and when you don’t)

Time slots make sense when physical capacity is a hard constraint or the experience demands dedicated time.

Cases where they’re essential

  • Museums and exhibitions with guided routes or safety limits
  • Corporate open days that include tours of production areas
  • Showrooms with one-to-one or small-group product demos
  • Restaurants for an event dinner with a fixed number of covers
  • Labs and workshops with a maximum number of participants per facilitator
  • Health screenings, mass vaccinations, public services
  • Theme parks and attractions with managed waiting times

Cases where you don’t need them

  • Conferences and talks in a single room with plenty of seating
  • Free, open-admission events with ample capacity
  • Parties and social mixers where free flow is part of the experience
  • Hybrid events with a dominant digital component

Rule of thumb: if the ratio between expected demand and simultaneous capacity is greater than 3:1, slots are necessary. Between 1:1 and 3:1, they’re recommended to improve the experience. Below 1:1, they’re just useless overhead.

The 3 time-slot management models

Every event fits one of three basic models. Choose the right one before you design your booking flow.

Model 1 — Fixed slots of uniform length

How it works: you split the event into slots of equal length (e.g. 30 min, 1 hour, 2 hours). Each attendee books one and only one slot. All slots have the same capacity.

When to use it: standardized, repeatable experiences. A museum visit with a guided tour, an identical product demo for every group, health-screening sessions.

Pros: simple to communicate, easy to run, allows staff and resources to rotate. Cons: low flexibility, doesn’t adapt to different visitor profiles.

Model 2 — Flexible, self-selected slots

How it works: you define a window (e.g. “10:00 to 18:00”) and the attendee books an arrival time, then stays as long as they like up to a maximum allowed duration.

When to use it: variable-length experiences where the attendee decides how long to stay. Trade fairs, showrooms, free-roam exhibitions with staggered entry.

Pros: comfort for the attendee, less friction at checkout. Cons: it’s harder to control actual density in the room; it requires active monitoring.

Model 3 — Multi-slot (booking several slots)

How it works: an attendee books multiple slots on the same day or across the event window, typically tied to different experiences. E.g. “Product A demo slot at 10:00” + “Workshop B slot at 14:30.”

When to use it: complex, multi-section events. Corporate open days with themed rooms, cultural festivals with several activities, conferences with break-out sessions.

Pros: a high level of personalization — the attendee builds their own agenda. Cons: a more complex booking-form UX, the risk of partially empty slots, and the need for a platform that can handle slot combinations in the cart.

How to size capacity per slot

This is the most common operational question. The practical formula is:

Capacity per slot = (maximum simultaneous capacity) × 0.70 × (slot duration / average experience time)

The 0.70 factor leaves a safety margin for: transition queues, attendees who linger beyond their slot, and large groups who want to stay together.

Worked examples

Event Maximum capacity Slot duration Average time Capacity/slot
Museum with guided route 50 people 60 min 45 min 26 people
Showroom open day 80 people 30 min 20 min 37 people
Event-dinner restaurant 150 covers 2 hours 90 min 140 people
Training workshop 30 seats 120 min 100 min 25 people

The 3 rules you must never break

  1. Never exceed the venue’s physical capacity for any reason — not even if “it’ll just about fit”
  2. Leave at least a 10–15% buffer for late arrivals, walk-ins and special guests
  3. Check cumulative capacity across the day: 10 slots × 30 people = 300 total attendances — is that a number your catering, security and restrooms can handle?

Managing no-shows and overbooking

The typical no-show rate for time-slotted events (free ones) is 15–25%. For paid events it drops to 5–10%. How you handle this determines the event’s margin.

Strategy A — Accept the no-shows

No specific mechanism. If a slot has 30 people booked and 22 show up, that’s fine. Suited to: cultural events, corporate open days, sightseeing tours.

Strategy B — Controlled overbooking

You accept more bookings than your real capacity, counting on no-shows. E.g. capacity 30 → you sell 35 seats. If 32 show up, you manage with rollover. If 35 show up, the extra 5 move to the next slot (if there is one) or get a refund.

Golden rule: overbook by no more than 15% above capacity, and only if your historical no-show rate exceeds 20%. Otherwise the operational risk outweighs the benefit.

Strategy C — Automatic waiting list

When a slot is full, the attendee joins a waiting list. If someone cancels, the platform notifies them automatically and gives them X hours to confirm. Suited to highly sought-after events with strong demand.

What to look for in a platform: native support for waiting lists with automatic email notification. Ticketto, Weezevent and Eventbrite all handle it — check how it’s configured before you launch.

Communicating with the attendee

A time-slot system fails more often because of confusing communication than because of technical problems.

Pre-event communication checklist

  • [ ] Immediate confirmation email with the booked slot front and center (time, duration)
  • [ ] 24-hour reminder with the slot time in the subject line
  • [ ] Change policy: can the user switch slots? Until when? How?
  • [ ] Lateness policy: what happens if you arrive 10 minutes late? 30? Is the ticket still valid?
  • [ ] Logistics: arrive 5–10 minutes early, where to check in, what to bring

A common mistake to avoid

Using vague language like “around 10:00” or “from 10 onwards.” Time slots only work with pinpoint precision in your communication. “Your slot runs from 10:00 to 10:45. Please arrive at the entrance at 9:55” is the level of detail required.

What to look for in a time-slot platform

Not every platform supports time slots in a serious way. Before you sign up, check these seven points.

  1. Configurable capacity per individual slot (not just a global limit)
  2. Controlled overbooking with a customizable threshold
  3. Automatic waiting list with email notification when seats free up
  4. Multi-slot in the cart (if you’re using Model 3)
  5. Slot changes by the attendee up to X hours beforehand
  6. Per-slot check-in (operations guide here): staff can see at a glance whether the attendee arrived at the right time
  7. Per-slot reporting after the event: theoretical capacity vs. actual attendees, for each slot

Time slots are a specialization of the registration form: to optimize the form itself, see our guide to the event registration page that converts.

If you want a broader picture of what a ticketing platform should do beyond time slots, we’ve written a complete guide.

Conclusion

Time slots aren’t a technicality — they’re an experience-design choice. When they work, the attendee doesn’t even notice them: they simply walk in, enjoy the event, and leave satisfied without ever feeling the pressure of a crowd. When they don’t work, they become the first thing the attendee remembers (for the wrong reasons).

The three critical points are: realistic capacity sizing, a clear policy on no-shows and lateness, and precise communication with the attendee before event day.

Ticketto natively supports all three time-slot management models, with configurable per-slot capacity, an automatic waiting list and per-slot check-in — a Pro-plan feature. If you want to see it in action, create your free account and activate Pro to set up your first slotted event: it takes 5 minutes.

entry.title: 10 Corporate Event Mistakes to Avoid
entry.content:
In short: organizing a corporate event isn’t a test of creativity, it’s a test of discipline. The 10 mistakes you’ll read below are the ones I’ve watched repeat dozens of times over 15 years — always the same ones, in different companies, with different budgets. At the end of the article you’ll find a downloadable operational checklist that prevents them all.

A premise: the problem isn’t creativity

Failed corporate events don’t fail for lack of ideas. They fail because someone took something for granted: that the venue was big enough, that the registration form was simple enough, that the speaker would actually show up. The vast majority of disasters come from operational mistakes, not from a deficit of vision.

Ten years ago I thought it was different. Then I watched an €80,000 convention collapse over acoustics that had never been tested, and a 300-person kick-off where half the attendees had no idea where to park. That’s when I started keeping a list. Here are the ten mistakes on it, ranked by how often they happen.

Mistake #1 — An undefined objective (or one defined uselessly)

“We want to run an event for the Sales team” is not an objective. It’s an intention. Without a measurable KPI (number of pipeline opportunities opened, internal NPS >8, X demos booked in the following 30 days), you’ll never know whether the event was a success — and so you’ll never know whether to repeat it, improve it or scrap it.

How to avoid it: write the objective in a single sentence with at least one number in it. If you can’t, the event isn’t ready to launch yet.

Mistake #2 — A rough budget with no contingency buffer

The first draft of a budget is almost always 15-25% too optimistic. Catering underestimates quantities, AV discovers cables that need renting, a last-minute vendor turns up to replace the one who didn’t. If your budget is “to the cent” with no margin, you’re heading for an overrun.

How to avoid it: ring-fence 20% of the budget as a contingency reserve — an extra 20% declared up front to the internal sponsor. Better to give some of it back than to ask for a top-up.

Mistake #3 — Choosing the timing without checking the real calendar

Launching a company kick-off on the Monday after Easter. Running a sales convention on the first Friday in August. Scheduling a training day on the day of an announced transport strike. All real cases, all avoidable.

How to avoid it: before locking in the date, check national and local public holidays in the target area, the typical quiet or peak periods for the sector (mid-summer slowdowns, the retail crunch in December), recurring annual transport disruptions, and competing events in the same city. 30 minutes of research saves weeks of damage control.

Mistake #4 — Choosing a venue without a site visit

The photos on the website always have sunshine. You can’t hear acoustics from a sales PDF. The stated capacity is the “standing at the buffet” figure, not the real number for a seated dinner. Rooms that look perfect in the brochure are often unsuited to what you actually want to do with them.

How to avoid it: always do a physical site visit with a technical checklist (natural light, acoustics, Wi-Fi tested with a speed test, parking measured in actual spaces, a kitchen with the right capacity, numbered restrooms, step-free access for wheelchair users). If you can’t go yourself, send a colleague with a written checklist.

Mistake #5 — A registration form with too many fields

Every extra field in the sign-up form drops your completion rate by 3-5%. You ask for name, email, company and role: do you really also need dietary requirements, t-shirt size, car transfers, special needs and a marketing newsletter opt-in, all on a single screen? No. You ask for those things later, in a follow-up communication.

How to avoid it: an initial registration form with 4-5 fields maximum. Everything else goes into a personalized email one week before the event. To dig into the patterns, we’ve written a guide to how a ticketing platform is structured. On the specific design principles of a page that converts, we have a guide to the event registration page with conversion-rate benchmarks by event type.

Mistake #6 — Unsegmented invitees

Sending the same “we’d like to invite you to the convention” email to the CFO and to a first-year junior produces dismal engagement in both directions. The CFO feels treated like just anyone; the junior feels out of place.

How to avoid it: segment your invitees into at least 3 tiers (senior management, middle management, operational staff) and tailor the subject line, the communication angle and the relevant internal agenda for each.

Mistake #7 — Weak pre-event communication

After registration, silence. Then an email the day before saying “see you tomorrow”. This approach produces a no-show rate of 15-25%, mainly because people forget or can’t find the practical details (exact address, parking, dress code).

How to avoid it: a minimum sequence of 3 automated communications — 2 weeks before (confirmation and agenda), 3 days before (a reminder with practical info), 1 hour before (a practical message by SMS or email). No-shows typically drop to 5-8%.

Mistake #8 — A disorganised check-in

A 10-minute queue at the entrance, staff with paper lists, attendees asking “do I sign here?”. Check-in is the first physical experience of the event, and if it goes badly it contaminates everything that comes after.

How to avoid it: digital check-in with QR codes and a smartphone app for the staff (we’ve written the complete operational guide). Average check-in time: 10 seconds. Stations: 1 for every 400-500 expected attendees, plus one as backup.

Mistake #9 — An overloaded agenda with no breaks

Eight 45-minute talks back to back with no interruption. Three consecutive panels in the afternoon. A 3-hour workshop with no break. After 90 minutes average attention collapses, and the rest of the program is lost.

How to avoid it: a 15-20 minute break every 90 minutes of content, ideally in an area away from the main room. After lunch, keep the content light or interactive (no heavy keynotes — digestion works against attention).

Mistake #10 — No post-event measurement

The event ends, the badges are collected, the vendors are paid, everything gets filed away. The following year you start from scratch, with the same mistakes. Without feedback data, every event is an island.

How to avoid it: within 24 hours of the event, send a short survey (5 questions maximum, 3 minutes to complete) with NPS, an open question — “what would you improve?” — and one closed question specific to the stated objective (mistake #1). Typical response rate with automated sending: 30-50%.

📋

The definitive corporate event checklist
